A self-ridden personality can show up throughout your everyday life, with a tendency to overrisk, try too hard, fear the possibility of getting laid out, or lose control over what you can do. We’ve found that this anxious tendency can have significant negative effects on productivity, because people tend to be more focused on getting money out of their pockets than on personal goals.

What’s the best way to fix it?

Develop a budget. Identify how much money you’re willing to spend over the course of any given year in your life. Identify what kind of money you’re willing to invest, from housing to real estate to student loan.

3. Self-government

What it means:

If such a man had anything more important to his life than governing himself, he would be in despair.

—Frank Franklin

If you’ve never heard of the concept of self-government, or anything in general, you’re not alone. Here’s the definition of self-government: “To manage yourself without any intervention or authority from others.” It sounds like the philosophy of “governing yourself” isn’t bad enough, because some people misconize it as something to be crazy about, but in a sense, self-government is like pot poker, a game in which all players are allowed to either kill each other or destroy each other.

What’s the best way to fix it?

Identify what kind of money you’re willing to spend. Identify what kind of house you’re willing to buy. Make sure you know where you’ll get one and if it’s right for you. Identify what loans you won’t take out of you. Identify whether you really have an underlying reason for buying something in the first place. If you’ve never owned a house, you’re well ahead of the game, but you’ll have to learn a thing or two from your experience.

4. Self-regulation

What it means:

The purpose of regulation is to do whatever it is best for you, not to leave it to the law again.

—John Adams

There’s a myth that has run throughout centuries of popular culture that the real source of regulation is the courts, a judge who has the power to force individuals to do whatever they want. The opposite is generally true: Most people assume that they’re intending to regulate themselves, and research suggests that this is simply wrong: The more regulated you are, the more uncomfortable you feel about yourself. Studies have shown that people who excessively regulate themselves are more likely to suffer from post-traumatic stress, feel isolated, and have higher rates of depression. The more regulated you think yourself, the more negative feelings and emotions you have; you don’t know where the regulation is coming from.

What’s the best way to fix it?

Decide that you’re intending to regulate yourself. Identify what you should invest in your life, from a loan to a new car to real estate. Write down your plan, including some resources and the tools you’ll need if you’re willing to proceed, and explain what it’ll take to get where it is. Be committed to your motivations, and cancel your plan when the stakes are high. Don’t give up your plan if you’re stressed or worried about the possibility of losing a job in your life.

What’s the best way to fix it?

Plan differently. Figure out what you really are interested in, and choose the tools that will help you reach your final goal. Stick to your original path. Experiment with different kinds of people and follow your way along. When you do get there, be sure to use some positive lessons you’ve learned from your experience to reach long-term goals.

5. Self-comfort

What it means:

Self comfort is something inside and outside, something you do not have. If you do not put it in place, you will look like an ignorant rask, or a lazy, uncooperative wanderer waiting for relief.

—James Franklin

What’s the way to fix it?

Be active. Leverage every opportunity to become more comfortable: Spend hours talking with people, playing with friends, sharing with family, communicating with students, and playing with fellow students. Don’t allow others to dig their heads in your face and pretend that they are smarter than you. Over time, the more you realize how comfortable you are, you can start increasing your capacity to interact with the outside world.

What’s the best way to fix it?

Become more comfortable by combining your personal and private life. Direct your attention to doing the things that matter to you, not letting others think about you. Become more creative by being willing to take small risks. Evolution your behaviors to become more productive and efficient. Try new rules and create your own. Lay out goals and aspirations that fit your personal needs. Take every opportunity you choose to share yourself with others.

The Lib Dems, which became a coalition member in June, say they will not support any measure that would drive the NDP out of power and have urged MPs to wait until after next election to decide whether they prefer staying in the coalition.Multiple sclerosis syndrome (MTS) is a mental illness that affects 40,000 people globally. Common symptoms of people with MTS include anxiety, distraction, pain, attention loss, and depression. Many of the patients with MTS have mutations that are caused by genes in their immune system. Once diagnosed and treated by a doctor, these mutations can lead to behavioral disorders such as depression, attention loss, anxiety, distraction, and impaired social relationships. Traditional medical approaches to treating MTS have included meditation, relaxation, consulting programs, and comprehensive therapy. However, over the past decade, there have been dozens of drugs designed specifically for the needs of MTS patients, but none have been effective. Many of these drugs have been found to have limited effectiveness, and although some of them have proven great potential, none have been found to work in patients with MTS. Psychazepam is a difficult drug to use, but can reduce activity of the dopamine cascade, a group of neurons located in the brain. Psychazepam use in MTS patients is recommended because of the harmful side-side effects and the potential for addiction.NEW YORK (Reuters) - U.S. stocks fell to their lowest levels for nearly 50 years on Wednesday, driven by growing doubt over the ability of the Federal Reserve Fund to write its own monetary policy and a sharp downturn in the U.S. stock market.

Customers hold their hands as they wait for a meal at Joe's McDonald's, a McDonald's restaurant in Los Angeles, California May 4, 2008. REUTERS/Janico De Riva

The fall spread elsewhere in the United States as the stock market plunged particularly sharply, and metal prices rose a sign that there was a concern over the Fed’s ability to buy up oil, gold and stock prices.

Industrial output, housing sales and U.S. stocks fell nearly 30 percent in the third quarter, according to the Standard John Meroney’s Index, which hit its lowest in nearly 50 years. Gross domestic product grew 4.1 percent in the second quarter of 2008 - the highest real-time growth since 1997.

Investors are growing skeptical about the central bank’s ability to write its own monetary policy draft, saying it’s likely to inflict a wound on the United States economy.

The Fed has imposed 3.6 trillion extra dollars a month for more than a decade to curb inflation and speed the economy’s recovery. It laid off its top executive in January but quickly reorganized its board and promised to introduce its own monetary policy within the next few months.

“The Fed has always been in an open position and open to making difficult policy decisions on the basis of its own interests,” said David Burkhart, head of market research at Gold Sachs, a firm in New York. “This time around around, it seems to have chosen to remain silent rather than aggressive.”

The fall was accompanied by moves in commodity prices.

Oil, the world’s largest source of crude, rose 13.1 percent to $2.29 a barrel on Wednesday, the fastest rise since a 10-year low in October.

That increase followed a meeting in London by Fed Chairman Benanke, who gathered with senior advisers to the President Barack Obama, to discuss plans to strengthen monetary policy in the interests of stabilizing the price of the world’s oil.

Gold, another key commodity, rose 11.3 percent to $0.78 a barrel on Wednesday, hitting its lowest level in 50 years.

BANKER SHOWS

The decline sent a particular shock to Wall Street banks, which have been struggling since the Fed began cutting protections in their balance books and rolling out of trillions of dollars in mortgage loans.

“Wall Street is basically becoming the rat on the face of the United States,” said Paul Morrissey, chief executive economist at Capital Strategies, a Washington-based research firm.

“If the Fed is able to actually change its monetary policy in real time, there will be massive capital losses to these banks. This is bad news for Wall Street because it is hurting investors and the American economy.”

Oil companies also took the fall for granted. Exxon Energy, which has said it will cut domestic production to drive down the price of its commercially profitable offshore coal fields, has blamed the slowing global oil prices on the recent collapse of the euro.

And in the name of health care for all.”WASHINGTON (AP) -- The House of Representatives on Tuesday unanimously approved legislation to prevent federal regulators from spying on medical marijuana businesses, which could be up for a debate in December.

The House unanimously voted 38-4 to pass the bill, the Property Tax Act, that would ban federal regulators from targeting businesses, and require that medical marijuana businesses must undergo "extensive financial, social and environmental assessment before they are approved for medical use."

The legislation will go to the House floor by the end of the month and the House Oversight Committee is expected to begin its work next week. lawmakers said the bill would mean the measure could be up for debate in December.

There is no word on when the legislation will be up for debate, but one source told Reuters that the Federal Bureau of Investigation will review the matter before making decisions.

Sheila Clark, a spokeswoman for Public Policy Watch, a nonprofit advocate for stricter medical marijuana laws, said that the bill's passage marks "an important step in a legislative process designed to protect [marijuana] patients and their families."

"Studies in recent years have found little evidence linking medical marijuana with drug-induced behavior, which is particularly common among patients suffering from alcohol abuse and addiction," Clark said.

The legalization of recreational marijuana has been complicated by partisan divisions over the topic in recent years, with lawmakers in at least 50 states having discussed the issue throughout the legalization process. As of last week, recreational marijuana is already legal in 49 states.

Opponents of the property tax measure dismissed the idea that the bill would simply interfere with local tax revenue.

"To me, it is unconstitutionable to force people who support the marijuana industry to pay taxes to fund it," said Rep. Jeff Grassman, D-Mass., a leading opponent of the property tax.

The Obama administration filed a proposal in January that would ban federal regulators from targeting marijuana businesses unless they undergo extensive financial, social, and environmental assessment before they are legally approved for medical use.

Only three states, Colorado, California, and Washington, have legalized recreational marijuana, though New York began legalized recreational use in July. Two states, Massachusetts and Oregon, have legalized religious marijuana.WASHINGTON (AP) -- A class lawsuit against a telecommunications company over its program to spy on customers' personal information is close to settling, after a federal judge on Monday left the matter open for trial.

The case, Cisbell Communications Services Inc. v. Sinclairbell, now goes to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Washington.

Cinsbell, which formerly belonged to Time Warner and Verizon, has been using technology to sneak into the personal information of millions of Internet customers for years. Plaintiffs have long alleged that the company has been digging into the personal data of those customers, including their names, addresses, Social Security account numbers and phone numbers since 2007.

The class lawsuit has been the most intense legal battle against the company since October 2010, when a three-judge panel in the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected an initial complaint filed by Ciscobell and a coalition of plaintiffs.

"The plaintiffs have an obligation to protect privacy, consumer safety and our constitutional values," wrote Justice Maureen L. Edwards in the ruling, which now leaves the matter open for trial. "Their concern is that such surveillance programs are posing an unacceptable threat to U.S. consumer privacy, which negatively affects our economic growth."

The government initially argued that it had an "independent duty" to hear the plaintiffs' complaints, but a majority of the judges upheld the lower court's decision, ruling that the agency had "neither intent nor authority to prevent (plusuit claims) from hearing their complaints."

The case was later referred to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which denied the government's request for an immediate hearing. The appeals court denied that request, ruling that the program was incompatible with constitutional protection under Title II of the Patriot Act of 2008.

For more information about Tyylle Wood, visit www.TyylleWood.co/EECRA, Sept 26 (Reuters) - Egyptian President Bashar Assad demanded justice for those who killed 13 people and injured dozens in an attack in Cairo on Sunday, and called on international leaders to step up intervention to ensure the return of peace over the country’s civil war.

“We call upon all concerned nations and institutions, including the Church of Egypt, to act on a legal basis, with due force and without delay, to bring justice to those responsible for this horrible and reckless attack, allegedly intended to destroy our nation’s infrastructure and recruit terrorists to attack our citizens,” Assad said in an interview at his presidential office in Cairo.

“We deeply condemn this horrific act and call upon the international community to intervene and take immediate action.”

The early-morning attack in central Cairo marked a dramatic expansion of the Egyptian civil war, which is now in its most unstable phase in its 15-year history.

Aggressive U.S. and allied military interventions have heightened tensions in recent months, with the rapid influx of Shi’ite Muslim militants into the country and a string of recent U.S. strikes, including an air strike on mosques in June.

Disconfusion over the motivation of the attack — the exact nature of the assailants and whether they carried arms — has contributed to worsening tensions with the Mouthi movement, which says it is led by Abu Fatah al-Baghazi, a Shi’ite Muslim religious leader.

The U.S. administration has promised to end the conflict by holding peace talks and driving President Mahmoud Abdul Sorsi out of power, but critics fear such moves would be an assault on the country’s stability.

U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton “strongly condemns the groups responsible in the incident, and demands that they take immediate action to avoid interfering with any progress towards a meaningful return to peace,” she said in a statement.

The United Nations Humanitarian Agency condemned the attack and said the majority of the victims were the civilian population, including men, women and children.

“All those allegedly responsible in the incident face investigation and brought to justice for their violations of international law, rule of law and freedom of expression,” the agency said in a statement.

Egypt’s military launched several responses to the attack, including car bombs, tear gas explosions and airstrikes. Authorities did not say how many people died.

A spokesman for Interior Minister Abdelfadel Malisi said there was no immediate motive for the attack, adding that several Mouthi leaders have previously threatened to drive Egyptian President Mahmoud Abdul Sisi out of power.

People display during a protest march in Telopolis, Egypt September 11, 2016. REUTERS/Muhad Abushar

The explosion occurred shortly after protesters took to the streets of capital Cairo to call for an immediate end to the country’s lingering civil war, urging Cairo to hold peace talks and restore stability.

The country, which is almost predominantly Sunni Muslims, has been plagued by sectarian divisions and heightened tensions between Shi’etite-majority Egyptians and the United States, Saudi and Gulf Arab countries.

The Nida movement, the country’s largest opposition party, took to its Twitter account condemning the attack, calling it “a vicious act of terrorism and an interference of security.”

“The deaths of civilians and those injured in this bloody explosionation only intensates our demands for immediate military intervention and an immediate end to all peace talks, as the civilian casualties serve as an inevitable blow to the hopes of a conflict-free Egypt,” Nida movement wrote on its website.

Saudi Arabia, which has endorsed the Mouthi movement throughout the conflict, also called the attack an “irresistible interference of security” and called on its allies to “act collectively.”

Saudi Arabia said the attack took place after airstrikes hit the most sensitive areas, such as central Cairo and the southern city of Azra, targeted by protesters. Another airstrike struck a building near a government headquarters, killing about 10 people, according to the Saudi news agency Al Jazeera.

Egypt has been stuck in civil war since 2006, when a peace deal fell short because of sectarian divisions among leaders and the heavy presence of militants in the Egyptian army.

Over the past three years, Egypt’s bombings, shooting and airstrikes have killed more than 100,000 civilians and held 3,157 hostages in the conflict, according to the U.N. Committee on Human Rights.

U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry said on Twitter the United States would “remain in contact” with Egypt amid tensions over the country’s civil war. Mouthists, who helped remove Egyptian President Abdel Bashar al-Sisi from power in 2011, have been organizing protests across Cairo for the past few weeks to demand a political solution.

Leave us your thoughts in the comments below.CHINA (Reuters) - Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Friday that Beijing must further expand its relations with Iran, which aims to increase levels of confidence and acceptance in the international community with respect to talks to end the country’s nuclear programme.

Chinese President Xi Jinping attends the launch of the annual G-20 summit at Wunderellberg in Berlin, Germany, February 18, 2016. REUTERS/Barat Saar

Xi told a regular news conference in Beijing that the G-20 summit, which focuses on discussing global policy and national security, “must concentrate on ending Iran’s nuclear programme and translating this goal into the solution of its political, economic, security, and regional problems”.

He added: “China must develop a strategy for further expanding its relations with Iran to increase confidence and acceptance with respect to nuclear talks and to encourage co-operation with the international community.”

“China must continue its co-operation with the international community on this issue to strengthen its political stability and position in a time of economic growth,” Xi said.

China has repeatedly pressured world governments and allies to delay nuclear talks, and it even successfully convinced the UN Security Council to pull out the Geneva nuclear talks in 2014, where Tehran pleaded guilty to possessing four nuclear bombs.

The United States, European Union and Russia have pressured Iran to end its nuclear programme, and have repeatedly called on Western countries to impose economic sanctions on Tehran unless they force it to roll back its nuclear weapons programme.

Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a closed-door meeting at their family farm in Moscow on Friday to try to maintain their close ties, according to state news agency RIA.

A Russian Foreign Ministry spokesman described the meeting as “a statement of friendship between our two countries” and emphasized the importance “of our joint effort to increase our capacity to achieve mutual goals on all fronts of world security”.

The news agency reported that Putin had asked Xi to be the lead advocate for stronger economic sanctions against Iran, which has opposed Western efforts to impose tighter controls on its nuclear weapons programme.A new study found that there are 11 common forms of “fear” that are most likely to negatively affect your health.

Adamar al-Abdanini, a Syrian journalist working for the European Observatory on Human Rights, was reportedly detained while reporting on human rights violations committed in the territory now controlled by the Islamic State (IS).

UK-based advocacy group Human Rights Watch (EWR) said Saturday that Abdenini, in the western city of Idascus, Syria, was detained by Iraqi security forces on April 31. He, as well as other Syrian and foreign journalists, were investigating serious human rights violations committed by the ethnic Ahdar tribes in the region, which has struggled since Syria secured independence from Turkey in 1994.

Abdenini, 38, is a director of the European Observatory on Human Rights, which represents journalists and political activists in besieged areas that have come under “mass occupation” by the Islamic State.

“Abdenini was detained while covering the spread of IS territory near the Syrian government’s capital, Idascus, and banned from arriving at the scene by Iraqi forces,” EWR said. “He was banned from communicating with Observatory staff, thus tortured for about three hours. He was transported to another location to be monitored for about two hours and then for another 30 minutes, until he was detained once more.”

A spokeswoman for the UN watch group could not be reached for comment.

IS’s 18-month war, which is declared a war crime by the UN Security Council, has sparked months of heavy fighting and bombing across much of Syria, Iraq, Lebanon, Lebanon and Yemen in violation of a ceasefire between Turkey and the U.S.-led alliance of Russia, Iran and China.A Democratic senator has stepped down as chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee amid growing concerns about its surveillance program, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Sen. Gary Carter, D-Mass., announced via a press release that he was leaving the committee due to personal reasons and being unable to find work.

"Today, I am stepping down as chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, due to growing concerns about its process and institution," Carter said in the press release. "While I deeply regret the impact of this decision on my colleagues, I have decided to continue my job, and I am committed to doing all I can to ensure the Senate remains an independent institution that emphasizes freedom of expression, democracy, due process and the exchange of views with people around the world."

Under Senate rules, senators must decide whether they should chair the committee by July 30, and a senator can choose to step down from the committee by August 23.

Carter has served in the Senate since 2001, when he chaired an investigation into violations related to the National Security Agency's collection of phone records of political targets after the September 11 terror attacks. He was executive director of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and served as chief of staff for George H.W. Bush in 2002 and George H.W. Bush in 2008. He also served as Vice President Joe Biden's chief of staff in the Obama administration.

Carter's resignation raises pressure for Democratic leaders around the country, who have been pushing for legislative reforms even as they lose battles for seats on the House Select Committee on Science and Technology. Sens. Chris Lewis, D-N.Y., Dan Mulakert, R-S.I., and Sen. Ann Schumer, D-S.C., have all left the committee as part of growing calls for the panel to release more detailed information about the intelligence community's massive surveillance program.

"It's one thing that we want information to be made public, but it is also absolutely important that Congress be held to account for the thousands of warrants that are being handed out to intelligence agencies for threats to our democracy," Carter said in the press release. "That we have to do that is completely at conflict with our democratic principles."

Democratic members of Congress around the country have been pushing for the panel to release more detailed information about its surveillance program. Largely inspired by the 1930s novel François de Carule, Zissandijo’s story takes place in 1920s New York, where the music scene is overrun by overcompetition and overparression. The picture’s horror themes are further extended by the everyday lives of its characters, who are struggling to deal with the pressures of this rock-and-roll cultural age. At the center of the story is Clyde (Brady Thomas), a wild-minded rapper who quickly rises to fame on the New York street music scene. But as Clyde’s self-driven pursuits—and his desire to become a megillionaire in hip-hop—prove increasingly unnegotiable to his friends and family, Clyde finds himself increasingly addicted to his music. Every night, he finds himself reading roorgy Internet magazines, playing noodzy drug-smorting video games and filling his parents’ cupboards with dogy sweets. By immersing underground hip-hop into everyday life, Zissandijo has allowed Thomas to focus on the characters’ desperate struggle for self-acceptation and turn it into an entertaining comedy.

A government aimed at regulating the sale of genetically modified crops in Scotland has passed a bill that allows farmers to sell crops without requiring a planting licence.

The bill will allow farmers to sell their crops by using GMO or Monsanto-based products, chemical or pesticides, without requiring planting licences or other regulatory approval processes.

Farmers will also be able to conduct environmental testing to ensure that crops are "safeely sold".

At present, genetically modified crops are illegal to sell commercially unless farmers are in compliance with relevant regulations.

The move was praised by the Food and Wine Association Scotland, which is supporting the Bill.

A spokesman said: "This bill is an important win for the food and wine industry.

"Farmers are experts at producing properly-preared crops. We believe this law will power families, ensure good food quality and save time and money."

Lord Michael Cochrane, chief executive of the Food and Wine Association, said: "The development and distribution of genetically modified crops has been causing enormous problems, and this Bill is a big win for Scotland's agriculture industry."In an event aimed at demonstrating how genetic engineering can transform our organs and make them lighter and healthier, the University of Michigan at Detroit is joining in with a new exhibition that will allow visitors to see what the university's research teams are doing to transform our health systems.

To start, UM researchers will be demonstrating the creation of cross-skin cells that can grow and proliferate, a process made possible by genetic engineering of a cell's DNA sequence. Additionally, UM scientists will be demonstrating new materials attached to shoes and shoes that make them lighter and easier to hold and wear.

"Genetic engineering is an exciting science, as it plays a key role in changing chemical structures in the body, improving our immune system and making us healthier and physically fit," said Nick Feale, associate professor of genetic engineering at UM. "The impact of genetic engineering on our organs and systems may be more radical than anything anyone has done in the past. This exhibition is an opportunity to explore the ways and means that we may be transforming our organs."

The exhibition also features UM scientists who will be working on two other projects: one to turn an artificial skin cell into an epidermal cell, and another to create a brand new, USB-attached tube that can connect a cell to an organ.

The exhibition event will be held on Thursday, July 29, at 6 p.m. at the Neuro Research Institute's headquarters, 1700 Palmer Park Drive, Detroit.

The plaintiffs, Americans Without Choice and the Center for a Free Press, filed lawsuits in the summer to stop AT&T from collecting phone records of people who use the high-speed broadband service and force the carrier to deny access to their personal information for at least 10 days.

AT&T and its competitors have made the argument that they are protecting their business interests by violating consumers' Fourth Amendment rights.

A bipartisan panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in Washington, DC, on Thursday ruled in favor of the Fourth Amendment lawsuit.

"Today's ruling is an important victory for Americans concerned about Internet privacy," David Gilger, the attorney representing one of the plaintiffs' lawsuits against AT&T, said in a statement. "By acting on their request, this court has put a halt on AT&T's plans to build a free, high-speed broadband network to hundreds of millions of connected Americans."

The hearing is scheduled to resume on July 31, though it is not clear exactly when that will take place. No further dates were given.These days it's easy to hear the terms like “downressed” and “disawareized,” or read about the epidemic of heart cancer, and wonder if there’s anything we have less to blame than depression.

Now a new group of researchers have offered some surprising answers to this common misinterpretation — namely, they found that the brains responsible for processing emotions may not just be what causes depression, but are essential in helping cause it.

Depressionism gets a lot of propaganda for its name (get your hands on HBO’s Game of Thrones and you’ll know exactly what's really going on), but numerous studies have shown that depression is associated with a variety of symptoms, including emotional headaches, shock yawbles, anxiety disorder, social dissatisfaction and job loss.

Still, very little is known about what exactly is behind the rise in depressed symptoms.

“There’s enough evidence that the emotional nervous system is directly involved in depression, but there’s not a comprehensive understanding of how neural systems respond to depressed symptoms,” says David Mefano, an associate professor of psychology and neuroscience at New York University.

The latest research has shone some light on the subject.

In the new study, Mefano, Saki and colleagues interviewed 400 patients who had been diagnosed with depression. They were asked about sex, age, criminal history, school location, family size, drug use and any known history of depression.

Next, the researchers conducted magnetic imaging to find out how the relatively high levels of glucocorticin — a chemical widely known to regulate production of cholinergic acids in the brain — contribute to depressive symptoms.

Based on these results, the researchers found that in patients with low-degree depression, the group showed a significant decrease in activation of regions of the brain that are known to be responsible for processing emotions and triggering positive thoughts.

In contrast, in patients with high-degree depression, the researchers observed a decrease in activation of the prefrontal cortex, which is essential for the cognitive recognition of an emotional-triggered thought.

More importantly, in patients with the diagnosis of moderate to very severe depression, the researchers observed a sharp decrease in activation of the premroplic cortex, which is known as a key tool in detecting and figuring out serious mental disorders, including anxiety, anxiety disorder and sleep disorder.

LONDON (Reuters) - India must do more to deal with climate change, the International Monetary Fund said Tuesday, citing concerns that global warming is stifling its country's growing economy and further aggravating inequality and poverty.

The fund urged the Indian government to put aside its clamures for radical policy reforms and adopt practical approaches to address climate change. It urged a coalition of international monetary institutions and developing countries to agree to a plan to cut carbon emissions from coal-fired power plants.

"The threat posed by man-made climate change is both real and imminent," said Caroline Drummond, the ICF's chairman. "A new approach to dealing with climate change should include greater assessment of climate risks, more detailed analysis of the impact of climate change on poverty, and greater agreement on the measures required to reduce poverty."

"India must work closely with other countries to deal with climate change, improve its transition to renewable energy and clean energy, and move quickly to reduce its dependence on fossil fuel sources and replace the increasingly heavy dependence on clean sources of energy from other countries," the report said.

The report also called on Indian officials to seek greater public awareness about the Shiv Chaturam - a religious holiday in Hinduism - and other measures to tackle poverty such as ending home debt, citing recent experiences in rural areas.

"The official presence of poverty in India has increased by a rate of 47 percent over the past 15 years. Effects of the financial boom have led to bursts in housing prices, instability in industry and land losses, resulting in marked reductions in living standards," the report said.

"Steeping poverty inequality is growing. Nearly half of the median income of Indian households is under 35; one third of them live on the fringes or unable to support their children; and a third of those who live in poverty have no access to basic means of income, such as food, health care and medical services."

The government has taken aggressive measures to stave off the renewable energy crisis. In 2008, it announced a plan to cut carbon emissions from coal-fired power plants, a move that has sat back for years.

Last year, India used 82 percent of the electricity consumed in cities across 35 states. Over the past two years, the government has cut the use of renewable forms of wind, electric and natural gas energy by 68 percent, officials said. The policy, met with widespread opposition from environmental groups, has cost the country's energy industry $36 billion, according to an industry analysis prepared by the central government.

While India remains deeply concerned about climate change, it has taken numerous measures to reduce its growing dependence on greenhouse gas emissions.

Last month, lawmakers agreed to a plan to cut carbon emissions from coal-fired power plants, and in March Congress approved a ban on the sale of solar energy from large power plants.

The researchers, led by Mark Lay of the University of Ottawa, Canada, and Hermann Morv of the Université International de La Paris, France, used a simple and efficient version of a conventional plastic-based manufacturing process to transform graphenes into tiny structures, randomly shaped structures strung between layers of graphene.

The team started out by treating a crystallized glass material with a half-meter-wide gap with a thick carbon dioxide solution very similar to an oxygen bar. To prevent graphenes from slipping into the gap, Morv and his colleagues applied a solution containing cyclohexane—a chemical important for protein formation in graphenes—heated the material over high heat for several minutes in a dedicated room. They added a solution containing ruthenium—a chemical element used in forming and holding graphene proteins—and injected it in the transformed material with an acetic acid. The resulting graphenes were transformed into tiny structures, estimated to be 10 to 20 times smaller than in the conventional method.

The team then divided the graphenes into smaller pieces and then separated them from the material using an electrical force.

By measuring the protein content of the graphenes, the researchers conducted radiation imaging of proteins in the tiny structures. They observed that the volume of graphenes in the structures increased significantly over the course of separation, compared with the conventional procedure, which typically only takes between two minutes and an hour.

This research has important implications for understanding the mechanisms of graphenes, as well as for expanding our knowledge of the chemistry and biology of graphenes. As the energy released by graphenes finds their way into cells, leading to medical potential, the technology could be used for diagnosis and treatment of rare diseases like cancer and leukemia.

Sander’s bill, S-285, would create a system in which students can still apply for a student loan upon graduation but only receive one if they have a median income between $65,000 and $80,000. This would dramatically improve the ability of student borrowers to access the system. It would make it more difficult for the federal government to prosecute loanholders who steal money from student loans, and it would provide more options for low-income families who are struggling to afford a home.

The proposal by Sanders represents the latest major development in the hot partisan debate over the “healthcare for all” to which Democrats traditionally refer. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-AVt., has repeatedly expressed support for “universal healthcare” as part of Obama’s health-care bill, and Sen. Marco Rubio, R-Fla., who is running for a spot on the Democratic National Campaign Committee, has been the leading opponent of “universal healthcare.”

From an economic perspective, Sanders is correct in his characterization that student debt is one of the biggest problems in American life. In addition to the sheer volume of student loan debt—which is now at its highest ever—high tuition, high costs of living, and high interest rates have made it increasingly difficult for students to get money off their pockets. Worst of all, student loan applicants have been subjected to incredibly complex procedures. Last year, the Washington Post published a shocking review of the procedures and found that in order to be eligible for a student loan, every applicant must pass through a wide array of authorities, including government officials, courts, universities, schools, labor unions, and employers. The process is at same simultaneously complex and frustrating.

Sander would simplify the problem, however, by requiring that students provide information before they actually apply for a loan. The proposal is a sort of sequel to the Affordable Care Act, which would have let students reject a loan request only after they learned more about the terms of the loan.

Sander’s proposal has drawn some critics who say his characterization is by no means correct.

“Almost everything he says in his bill is totally wrong,” Gabrielle Jones, the executive director of the Student Debt Alliance, an organization that fights the debt crisis in America, told HuffPost in an interview. “Whether you’re talking about mortgage or property or student loans, he’s totally wrong.”

The debt crisis has spread to just about every member of the U.S. household. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a household with a median income of anywhere between $65,000 and $80,000 can have between $10,000 and $20,000 in debt. It’s also increasingly difficult to secure a stable, affordable home. In a 2007 survey, the Goldman-Schman Center and the Southern Poverty Law Center found that 56 percent of Americans said their household had no access to a student loan, while 37 percent said their home had received no student debt.

The problem is even worse for low-income families, who account for more than one third of all student debt. With a median income of $2,750 or higher, students swallow up an estimated $16.8 trillion in student loan debt, according to the Government Accountability Office. This debt includes rising college and university tuition, rising property values, soaring rent rates, and expensive nongominal debts like student-aid payments and student-retation payments.

This massive debt burden has made it increasingly difficult to find an affordable home across the country—especially for low-income families. A study by the conservative Keene Law Center found in 2010 that only 19 percent of Americans have found an affordable home in their neighborhoods, and another report by the Pew Research Center found that 83 percent of Americans are missing an affordable home. To make matters worse, only 2 percent of college graduates have filed a housing claim.

And of course, that doesn’t mean it’s all that bad to have a loan on hand. A 2008 study by the Committee on Economic Cooperation and Government Accountability found that 99 percent of Americans make almost half their net income from snaging a student loan of some kind. Mark Silverman, a law professor at the Harvard School of Law, claimed in a major blog post that year that fewer than 5 percent of applications for student loans are granted. Of course, that isn’t true. That year, the Bureau of Education, which has evaluated student loan applications for over two decades, noted that the annual rate of failed applications is just 20 percent. A 2009 investigation by the New York Times examined the federal government efforts to maintain student loans and protect them from future crises, finding that it has spent at least $40 billion on defefering student loans and $120 billion to fund their maintenance.

A research team from Columbia University, Harvard, Penn University, Georgia University, and Stanford University have found evidence that a regular diet of pneumonia vaccine can improve heart activity in patients with chronic heart disease. Their findings are published online today in the Journal of Cardiology.

"The results are a clear indication of peppermint vaccine’s clinical potential," says Giulia Casilia, MD, MD, an associate professor of cardiology and heart medicine at Columbia and lead author on the study. "Previous studies have demonstrated the incredible effectiveness of plum vaccine in preventing cardiovascular disease and improving heart health, and our study now provides the first, conclusive evidence of its clinical and therapeutic potential."

In the new study, the team of researchers recruited a group of 32 women with chronic heart disease who received 50 mg of standard peppermint vaccine and 50 mg of animal-produced peppermint vaccine. After 24 weeks of regular plum vaccine injection, they reported a 20 percent increase in heart activity.

The results come after scientists had been wondering about whether peppermint vaccine could help people with chronic heart disease, which accounts for more than 80 percent of adults with chronic blood pressure and other heart diseases. Chronic heart disease is a cardiac condition that increases blood pressure, controls blood flow and affects the immune system, and is associated with symptoms of chronic pain, cardiac numbness, headache, breathing problems, and cardiac deterioration.

Each year in the U.S., approximately 1.7 million people have chronic heart disease, up from 1.4 million in 2012, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The annual mortality rate rose 40 percent between 1980 and 2013, and suicide rates doubled between 1994 and 2012, according to the National Institutes of Health.

"We were optimistic that the plum vaccine could slow down the side effects of chronic heart disease," says Patricia Mulcher, MD, MD, an associate professor of cardiology and cardiology at Georgia University, who was not involved in the study. "But we didn’t know how the vaccine would actually work, so it was interesting to see if the plum vaccine was more of a prevention aid rather than an adjuvant to heart disease."

The plum vaccine excrettes blood from the body’s liver and sends the blood back to the body’s central immune system called the plaxsia, which acts as an "inner door" to the body's heart. Beyond its role in helping people recover from chronic heart disease, the vaccine has been shown to slow down immune reactions in the heart as well as prevent various diseases from diabetes to chronic stress disorder.

In the new study, the researchers recruited a group of 32 women with chronic heart disease, all of whom were under 35. The women were injected with three variants of the plum vaccine: lab-produced, animal-produced, and genetically modified. After 14 weeks, the women treated with the lab variant reported a 18 percent increase in heart activity (which was compared to those who were not treated with the animal-produced vaccine).

Specifically, using an adjusted-time ratio (T-2) correlation test (A-s(p = 0.05), we controlled for daily body weight, food consumption (total per million calorie metres; SMD = 3.55), and a measure of the Body Fat Index, we found a significant correlation between weight and cancer risk (mean factor effect of 10 percentage points compared with a healthy control, n = 7 out of 63 participants). Multvariable variables, such as household size, education level, income, and living conditions, account for 25-30 percent of the nation’s poverty. These numbers alone show that Americans have to act at an accelerated pace to meet the needs of their citizens.

The Poverty Project, a government-funded community organization, is leading the path to solving the poverty crisis. Its mission is to end poverty, reduce homelessness, improve housing affordability, promote community participation, low-wage jobs, and reduce income inequality.

According to the project:

“The number of Americans who live in poverty is increasing and we need to reduce it. Our approach is to engage together with community leaders and give them ideas, suggestions and feedback on simple and practical solutions. For example, we are focused on improving school performance, improving energy efficiency, ensuring affordable housing, and improving public safety. We also reach out to local businesses, families, and citizens in order to work on these issues.”

The Poverty Project, founded in 2010, aims to bring together community leaders in response to an unprecedented level of poverty. It requires community leaders and volunteers to raise awareness about the problem, develop a strategic and policy plan, and work closely with local officials, state and federal agencies to overcome this crisis.
